title: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
intro: Scaling expands system capacity to handle increasing transaction volumes by either upgrading physical machine specs or clustering multiple commodity nodes.
objectives: Compare trade-offs between Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) and Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out).
Overcome stateful data bottlenecks using database read-replicas and sharding keys.
Configure autoscaling metrics and cooldown stabilization periods.
body:
### Vertical vs Horizontal Comparison
- **Vertical Scaling (Scale-Up)**: Upgrading CPU cores, RAM, and NVMe SSDs. Simple (zero architectural changes), but hits physical hardware limits, exhibits single point of failure (SPOF), and suffers from diminishing cost-performance returns.
- **Horizontal Scaling (Scale-Out)**: Adding commodity virtual machines or containers behind a load balancer. Near-infinite scalability and high fault tolerance, but demands distributed consistency, sharding, and network partition resilience.

### The Shared-Nothing Principle
State-of-the-art horizontal compute tiers adopt a **shared-nothing architecture**: each compute node operates independently with its own memory, delegating persistence to distributed databases (Postgres replicas, Cassandra, DynamoDB).
keyIdea: Scale compute horizontally with stateless containers; scale storage with read-replicas, partitioning, and caching.

concepts.title: Read-Replicas vs Sharding
concepts.body: Read-heavy workloads scale by adding asynchronous replicas. Write-heavy workloads require sharding data across multiple database primary nodes.

concepts.title: Autoscaling Throttling
concepts.body: Cooldown windows prevent flapping (rapid churn of adding/removing nodes during spiky traffic bursts).

examples: Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scaling pods based on CPU/memory target thresholds.

quiz.prompt: What is the primary constraint of scaling up vertically?
options: Hits physical hardware boundaries and creates a SPOF
quiz.explanation: Vertical scaling is bounded by the maximum specs of a single physical machine and represents a single point of failure.
